The Hong Kong Monetary Authority on Thursday unveiled an “ART” Framework under Fintech 2030 to help banks adopt artificial intelligence responsibly, as the technology evolves from generative tools to autonomous agentic systems. “ART” stands for accountability, resilience and trust. Accountability requires clear ownership and human oversight throughout the AI lifecycle. Resilience focuses on secure, robust systems that fail safely. Trust emphasizes fairness, transparency, explainability and privacy. “By pairing innovation with clear accountability, resilient operating models and effective human oversight, banks can fully realize the benefits of AI while maintaining the trust and stability of Hong Kong’s financial system,” said Arthur Yuen Kwok-hang, HKMA deputy chief executive. The HKMA noted that more than 60 per cent of the use cases explored agentic AI, reflecting the industry’s active pursuit of advanced applications such as automated planning and execution of multi-step tasks within defined boundaries and controls. Under the framework, the HKMA has issued an updated Supervisory Guidance for Responsible Adoption of Artificial Intelligence. The guidance outlines nine principles across the three ART pillars and draws on insights from the second cohort of the Generative A. I. (GenA. I. ) Sandbox. These principles replace the HKMA’s 2019 High-Level Principles on Artificial Intelligence and provide more detailed expectations on board-level governance, risk management, trust and transparency. In collaboration with Cyberport and the University of Hong Kong, the HKMA will also establish an A. I. training data sharing platform, with data quality assurance as a core design principle. It will further test agentic A. I. applications through the GenA. I. Sandbox++ and publish a discussion paper on a proposed supervisory framework for agentic A. I. governance. The paper will explore intent-anchored accountability, a registry of material A. I. agents, and effective intervention mechanisms. These steps build on the GenA. I. The systems built to catch financial crime generate so many alerts that the people reviewing them can barely keep up. Most of those alerts turn out to be false positives, yet each one still has to be opened, researched, documented, and closed. For years, the industry’s answer was simple: hire more analysts. That approach is running out of road. Payment volumes keep climbing, real-time rails leave no room for overnight review, and fraudsters now use automation of their own. The question for financial institutions is no longer whether to modernise their defences, but how far to let machines take over the work. - Advertisement -. The alert fatigue problem. Traditional fraud and anti-money laundering (AML) tools were designed around rules. If a transaction crosses a threshold, comes from an unusual location or matches a known pattern, the system raises a flag. That model is transparent and easy to explain to regulators, but it is also blunt. Rules tuned to catch more crime inevitably catch more innocent customers too. The result is a backlog that lands on Level 1 (L1) analysts, the frontline investigators who triage each alert. Their work is repetitive by nature: pull the customer profile, check transaction history, look for links to known bad actors, write up a rationale, and decide whether to close or escalate. It is skilled work, but much of it follows the same steps every time. Three pressures are making this model harder to sustain:. Real-time payments. Instant transfers settle in seconds, so suspicious activity has to be stopped before the money moves, not reviewed the next morning. More sophisticated fraud. Supervisors expect every decision to be documented and defensible, which adds time to every case. What modern fraud detection looks like. AI-powered personal finance startup Matters has emerged from stealth with $5 million in pre-seed funding to develop a consumer banking platform focused on helping users manage their spending and increase their savings. The round was led by Swedish angel investor Jakob Johansson, with participation from Knut Frängsmyr (former COO of Klarna), Douglas Stark (Voi co-founder), Johan Bladh (CEO of Röko), Patrik Tran (CEO of Validio), and Per Widerstrom (CEO of Evoke). Matters was founded by Per Österström with the aim of building an AI-native consumer bank that combines automation and personalised financial guidance to help customers improve their financial wellbeing. The company's planned offering combines neobank services with an AI Advisor designed to help users make more informed spending decisions, increase savings and work towards their financial goals. Customers will pay a flat monthly subscription fee, while revenue streams typically retained by banks, such as interchange revenue and foreign exchange fees, will be returned to users through an accumulated cashback system. Through this model, Matters aims to align its business interests with those of its customers, focusing on customer experience, retention and long-term loyalty. According to Österström, traditional banking models do not always encourage better financial decisions, while Matters intends to take a different approach by making financial wellbeing more accessible. Our goal is to build a bank that actively makes financial wellbeing available to anyone, not just those who already enjoy it,. he said, adding that the company expects to launch its first consumer product in the coming weeks. According to figures cited by Matters, half of Gen Z and millennials do not know where their money goes, while 80 per cent of young adults report experiencing regular financial stress. Matters aims to address these challenges through AI-powered financial guidance and automated tools. title: Deutsche Bank deploys on-premises AI platform across investment banking teams
excerpt: Deutsche Bank deploys on-premises AI platform across investment banking teams. By Dalvinder Kular 15/10/2026. Deutsche Bank has rolled out a new on-premises AI platform across its investment banking and capital markets teams in Europe and North America. The technology will be installed in partnership with technology company Farsight and aims to embed AI into client-facing workflows while keeping sensitive data within its own technology environment. The bank said the deployment enables bankers to apply AI to internal documents, proprietary data and established working practices without information leaving the bank's infrastructure. By running the technology on-premises, Deutsche Bank said it will maintain greater control over sensitive information while enabling AI to access the internal data and institutional knowledge needed to support investment banking workflows. The bank added the approach allows AI to be tailored to its own processes and standards, while ensuring proprietary information and workflow activity remain within its technology environment. The platform is designed to incorporate Deutsche Bank's existing materials, internal standards and team-specific processes, allowing employees to generate and refine presentations and other client documents through a conversational AI interface that learns from user feedback over time. The rollout has initially been deployed across Investment banking and capital markets teams in Europe and the Americas. George Tierney, managing director and global chief operating officer for M&A at Deutsche Bank, said: “Our teams have very specific standards for what goes in front of a client, and those standards vary from group to group. “The platform gives our teams a way to apply AI to their own workflows and materials while operating within Deutsche Bank's technology environment. That combination of control and customisation is critical to making AI work in a global, regulated enterprise like Deutsche Bank. ”. Share Story:.
